content:
Apple Watch two new features could violate privacy laws in multiple US states, as the new Live Rewind and Siri Recap features record conversations.

The devil is in the details — neither feature allows anyone to access the recordings, and it appears it will take a court test to establish new legal precedent…

Live Rewind and Siri Recap

Apple announced the latest Apple Watch models support four audio intelligence features using the built-in microphone:

  • Sound Recognition, which can identify sounds like doorbells, smoke alarms, and more
  • Music Recognition, powered by Shazam technology
  • Live Rewind, which can convert conversations you just missed into text
  • Siri Recap, which can provide high-level summaries of conversations

It is precisely the latter two features that have sparked privacy controversy, because they record everything said by you and everyone around you.

Recording Laws

The legality of recording and when it applies depends on the state or country.

Many US states adopt the so-called "two-party consent" rule, meaning all parties in a conversation must know and consent to it being recorded. In these states, using any device to record a conversation without the other party's knowledge or consent is illegal. (There are certain exceptions for law enforcement, but they are not relevant to this discussion.)

If the Apple Watch truly stores recordings and can play them back, the laws in these states are clear: consent must be obtained first. The complication is that Apple has explicitly stated this is not the case.

Apple's Privacy Measures

Apple has clearly put considerable effort into privacy, and we previously discussed how they introduced each feature.

Neither feature runs in the background by default and must be manually activated each time. Live Rewind must be reactivated every time it is used and only runs for 15 seconds. Recordings cannot be accessed by anyone and are stored only on an isolated encrypted chip.

Recordings are stored only briefly, used to generate transcripts or summaries, and then immediately deleted.

Legal Uncertainty

Despite the above measures, Bloomberg cited legal experts pointing out that these new features create legal uncertainty.

Bloomberg reporter Natalie Lung consulted attorneys in California, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and Washington on September 11. These states generally prohibit eavesdropping on private or confidential conversations without the consent of all participants… Without exception, the attorneys she interviewed considered Apple's safeguards insufficient to provide adequate liability protection for wearers… Even if conversations are merely processed continuously and no traditional recording is ultimately produced, it could still be considered eavesdropping under state law. Pennsylvania defense attorney Phil Lauer said the technology is "close to legal because no individual actually receives and uses the data." But he added it "could still be considered illegal" because the device is collecting and parsing audio. Lauer noted: "Given the various privacy protections Apple has implemented, whether a court would take the same view is an interesting question, and that question is about to arise."

9to5Mac's Take

This is another example of the law failing to keep up with technology. If recordings are used to generate transcripts or summaries, but no one can directly access them, does that constitute a violation of anti-recording laws? The short answer seems to be: no one knows.

Live Rewind in particular appears harmless. It only records the last 15 seconds of a conversation, and emits a prompt tone each time it is activated, even if the watch is in silent mode or connected to headphones.

Ultimately this issue will likely need to be tested in court. The dilemma facing Apple Watch wearers is: if the court rules that the new features fall under the relevant laws, the legal liability falls on the wearer, not Apple.
